meta.title: Ride Hailing
meta.summary: Match riders to nearby drivers in real time (Uber / Lyft style), with live location streaming and payment at trip end.

functional: Drivers stream their location while online
Riders request a ride and are matched to a nearby available driver
Driver accepts or declines an offer; rider sees the assigned driver and ETA
Fare is computed and charged when the trip ends
nonFunctional: A driver can never be assigned to two trips at once
Location updates every ~4 s per active driver
Each city keeps working if one zone fails

slos.name: Time to match
slos.sli: Ride requests with a driver assigned within the threshold, divided by all requests, measured by the matching service

slos.name: Trip API availability
slos.sli: Trip requests that succeed divided by all trip requests, at the load balancer

slos.name: Driver position freshness
slos.sli: Driver positions in the index newer than the threshold, divided by all online drivers

slos.name: Charged once
slos.sli: Completed trips charged exactly once, divided by completed trips, from nightly reconciliation

alerts.when: Unmatched requests above 10% for 5 minutes while drivers are available nearby
alerts.why: Riders are waiting and drivers are idle, which means matching is broken, not that supply is low.

alerts.when: Trip API errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Riders cannot request or complete trips.

alerts.when: Any trip charged more than once, found by reconciliation
alerts.why: It is money, and trust is hard to win back. Stop and fix.

alerts.when: More than 5% of online drivers have a position older than 20 seconds
alerts.why: Matching starts offering drivers who have already moved.

alerts.when: WebSocket disconnects above 3 times the normal rate for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Usually a gateway deploy or a network problem. Drivers drop out of the pool.

signals.name: Unmatched requests by reason
signals.why: Separates no drivers nearby from lock contention and map provider failures.

signals.name: Open connections per node
signals.why: A node near its limit drops connections and causes a reconnect storm.

signals.name: Position updates per second against expected
signals.why: A sudden drop usually means an app or gateway problem, not drivers going offline.

debug.symptom: Riders wait too long for a match
steps: Check supply and demand for that city: it may simply be too few drivers.
Open a slow match trace: nearby search, the maps ETA call, or the lock?
Check the maps provider latency and error rate.
Check geo index shard load for that city.
Check gateway connections per node: a node near its limit drops connections.
Check recent gateway deploys: draining connections too fast causes reconnect storms.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Geo routed: sends each app to its city's region

nodes.label: Load Balancer (L7)
nodes.description: Terminates TLS; keeps each WebSocket pinned to one gateway

nodes.label: WebSocket Gateway
nodes.description: Holds one persistent connection per online driver and rider

nodes.label: Matching Service
nodes.description: Finds and locks the best nearby driver

nodes.label: Driver Geo Index
nodes.description: In-memory index of available drivers by location (Redis GEO or H3 cells)

nodes.label: Location Stream
nodes.description: Every location ping, for trip tracking, ETA models and analytics

flows.title: Driver location update
flows.summary: Every ~4 s each online driver sends a position. This is the highest-volume path in the system.

steps.label: WS frame: location
steps.detail: Sent over an already-open WebSocket: no new connection or TLS handshake per update.

steps.label: same connection
steps.detail: The load balancer keeps each WebSocket pinned to the gateway instance that accepted it.

steps.label: GEOADD available:sf
steps.detail: Only the latest position matters, so this is an in-memory overwrite. ~250k writes/s fits a Redis cluster sharded by city; a disk-based database would struggle.

steps.label: append location event
steps.detail: The full history goes to a stream for live trip tracking, ETA models and analytics. The geo index stays small and hot.

flows.title: Request a ride
flows.summary: Find nearby drivers, rank by real road ETA, lock one so nobody else can take it, and offer the trip.

steps.label: resolve api.rides.example.com
steps.detail: Geo routing sends each app to its city's region, so the rider, the driver and the matching service for that city share a region. A short TTL lets traffic move if a region fails.

steps.label: INSERT trip REQUESTED
steps.detail: The idempotency key makes a retried tap return the same trip instead of creating two.

steps.label: GEOSEARCH 2 km
steps.payload: GEOSEARCH drivers:available:sf FROMLONLAT -122.4192 37.7793 BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 10

steps.label: 10 nearest drivers
steps.detail: Straight-line nearest, which is only a first cut.

steps.label: ETA matrix 10×1
steps.detail: Rivers, bridges and one-way streets make straight-line distance misleading, so candidates are ranked by road ETA.

steps.label: SET lock:d_7781 NX EX 15
steps.detail: Atomic claim. Two matchers serving two riders can never offer the same driver at once. The 15 s expiry frees the driver if they ignore the offer.

steps.label: push offer to d_7781
steps.detail: Routed to the gateway instance holding that driver's connection.

steps.label: UPDATE … WHERE status='REQUESTED'
steps.detail: Conditional update: if the rider cancelled meanwhile, zero rows change and the driver is released.
steps.payload:
UPDATE trips SET status = 'ACCEPTED', driver_id = 'd_7781'
WHERE id = 't_552' AND status = 'REQUESTED';

steps.label: driver arriving in 3 min
steps.detail: From here, the rider app follows the driver's position over its own WebSocket.

flows.title: Complete trip and pay
flows.summary: Compute the fare from the actual route, then charge exactly once.

steps.label: route distance + duration
steps.detail: Uses the recorded GPS trace, snapped to roads.

steps.label: fare = base + km + min × surge
steps.detail: Surge comes from supply and demand per city cell at request time; it was shown to the rider up front.

steps.label: charge, key = t_552
steps.detail: The trip id is the idempotency key: if the call times out and is retried, the provider returns the first result instead of charging twice.

steps.label: trip complete
steps.detail: The driver goes back into the available pool on their next location update.

notes.text: Shard by city (or by H3 / geohash prefix). A rider's search only touches one shard, and hot cities get more shards.
It holds only current positions, which drivers resend every 4 s. After a failover the index refills itself within seconds; nothing needs restoring.
WebSockets push offers instantly and avoid 1M clients polling. Cost: stateful connections, so gateways need connection draining on deploys and clients must auto-reconnect.
Nearest driver is not always best. Production systems batch requests for a second or two and solve a small assignment problem to lower total pickup time.
Payment provider down: mark the trip COMPLETED with payment pending and retry from a background job. Never block the driver's next trip on payment.

ALB vs NLB: an application (L7) load balancer handles WebSockets and adds TLS termination and path routing. At ~1M long-lived driver connections, many teams put a network (L4) load balancer in front of the WebSocket gateways instead: higher connection limits, lower latency, static IPs, and the gateways terminate TLS themselves.

Geo routing keeps a city in one region, which keeps the driver geo index and matching local. If a region fails, change the DNS answer and drivers reconnect to another region within a few minutes (about one TTL).

questions.q: Drivers send their location every few seconds. How do you handle that write volume?
questions.a: Treat locations as ephemeral: keep only the latest position per driver in an in-memory geo index, not a database row per update. Drivers stream over persistent WebSocket connections so there is no per-update handshake. The full history goes to a stream for analytics, off the hot path.

questions.q: How do you find nearby available drivers quickly?
questions.a: Index drivers by a geospatial cell such as a geohash or H3 cell, then look up the rider's cell and its neighbours. That turns a search over every driver into a few small lookups. Cell size is a trade-off: too large returns many candidates to filter, too small needs many neighbouring cells.

questions.q: Two riders are offered the same driver at the same moment. How do you prevent a double booking?
questions.a: Make the assignment an atomic claim: the driver's state changes from available to offered with a conditional write (compare-and-set) or a short lease. Only the request that wins the claim proceeds; the other moves to the next candidate. The trip record is created only after the driver accepts.

questions.q: A WebSocket gateway instance dies. What happens to the connected drivers and riders?
questions.a: Their connections drop and the apps reconnect, with backoff and jitter, through the load balancer to another instance. Nothing important lived only in the gateway: trip state is in the trip service and positions are refreshed by the next update. A connection registry is updated on reconnect so pushes reach the new instance.

questions.q: The payment provider times out at the end of a trip. Was the rider charged?
questions.a: You do not know, so never blindly retry a charge. Send every charge with an idempotency key tied to the trip, so a retry returns the original result instead of charging twice. Mark the trip as payment pending and reconcile with the provider asynchronously; the rider can leave immediately.

questions.q: How would you compute surge pricing?
questions.a: Aggregate supply (available drivers) and demand (ride requests) per geo cell over a short sliding window from the location and request streams. Price is a function of the ratio, smoothed so it does not flicker. It runs asynchronously; matching only reads the latest multiplier for a cell.
